submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires when the text conventionally designates something — an individual, place, kind or title is said to be called / known as / termed / described as / dubbed / nicknamed / referred to as ['the'] Y (Chinese 被称为 / 称为 / 俗称) — with the peak on the naming predicate (' called', ' known', '被称为') and/or on the determiner that opens the designation (' the Y'). It stays near zero on the phone/summon sense of 'call', on one-off naming of a particular person, on plain taxonomic labelling of an ordinary object ('My friend is called John', 'The teacher called the student a genius', 'The student was called a genius', 'The tool is called a hammer', 'The function is called the sigmoid function' — all ≤ 0.15 of the scan max), and on ordinary declaratives or plain copulas with no naming predicate; inside the frame the strength is graded, with habitual adverbs, definite designations and place/kind subjects reaching 0.5-1.4x the scan max.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The Great Barrier Reef stretches for more than two thousand kilometres along the north-east coast of Australia, from the Torres Strait in the north down to Lady Elliot Island in the south. It is not a single reef but a loose network of roughly three thousand individual reefs and about nine hundred islands, built up over many thousands of years by countless generations of tiny coral polyps. Each polyp secretes a hard skeleton of calcium carbonate, and as older colonies die new ones grow on top of them, so the whole structure slowly rises towards the surface and spreads sideways. The reef supports an astonishing variety of life. More than fifteen hundred species of fish have been recorded there, along with six species of sea turtle, thirty species of whale and dolphin, and hundreds of kinds of hard and soft coral. Small fish shelter among the branching corals, larger predators patrol the drop-offs, and at night the reef becomes a different place altogether, as shrimp, crabs and hunting fish emerge from the crevices.

For most of its length the reef lies well offshore, separated from the mainland by a shallow lagoon, though in places it comes close enough that you can wade out from the beach at low tide. Fishing boats, dive charters and tourist ferries cross the lagoon every day, and the towns along the coast depend heavily on the visitors who come to see the corals and the wildlife. Because of its extraordinary size and the diversity of life it supports, the entire system is often called the world's largest living structure, a phrase that appears in countless guidebooks and school textbooks.

That description is not entirely accurate. The reef is a collection of living things, but it also includes sand cays, rocky islands and deep channels where very little grows. Its size is measured in different ways depending on whether you count the whole marine park, the reef proper, or the chain of shoals and platforms that continues further north. Tourism alone is worth billions of dollars a year to the regional economy, and the reef is central to the identity of the communities that live beside it.

Water temperature matters enormously to corals, and unusually warm summers can cause the polyps to expel the algae that live inside their tissues and supply them with much of their food. When that happens the coral turns white, and if the heat persists the colony may die. Park authorities monitor the reef closely, restrict fishing in certain zones, and run programmes to control crown-of-thorns starfish, which feed on coral and can strip a reef bare when their numbers explode. Scientists also study how different coral species cope with warmer water, hoping to identify those that might survive long enough to reseed damaged areas. None of this work is simple, and none of it happens quickly, but the reef has survived ice ages and changes in sea level before, and those who study it argue that it can survive this century too, provided the water stays cool enough for long enough each year.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context holdout: the only designation ('is often called the world's largest living structure') sits roughly 400 tokens in, far beyond the 16-token window the attribution reports, and the hypothesis still predicts it should fire.
